Then I can separate the general Medicaid coverage rules from the CAP/DA-specific participation requirements.## General eligibility criteria for **CAP/DA** services

Under **Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2**, a person generally must meet both the **basic Medicaid eligibility requirements** and the **CAP/DA-specific participation criteria**.

### 1) Basic Medicaid eligibility
The policy says the beneficiary must:

- be **enrolled in the NC Medicaid Program**; and
- not have an **eligibility-category restriction** that makes them ineligible for CAP/DA services.

Source: **Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2, Section 2.1.1 — "General"** (effective Sept. 1, 2025)  
[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

### 2) General Medicaid coverage criteria
Like other covered services, CAP/DA services must be:

- **individualized and specific** to the beneficiary’s symptoms or confirmed diagnosis, and not excessive;
- able to be **safely furnished**; with no equally effective and more conservative or less costly statewide alternative available; and
- provided in a way **not primarily for the convenience** of the beneficiary, caregiver, or provider.

Source: **Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2, Section 3.1 — "General Criteria Covered"** (effective Sept. 1, 2025)  
[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

### 3) CAP/DA-specific eligibility / participation criteria
For **CAP/DA**, the beneficiary must meet the policy’s specific criteria, including:

- meet the required **HCBS nursing facility level of care (LOC)** as determined by NC Medicaid;
- require **long-term care support** at a level typically provided in an institution, tied to a documented medical diagnosis and functional care need;
- have a completed **CAP assessment** showing a **reasonable indication of need** for at least one CAP/DA HCBS service within **30 calendar days** of the evaluation;
- have a **signed service plan** authorizing one or more waiver services to be provided monthly, or authorizing short-term equipment/modification/technology to help the person remain in or return to the primary private residence;
- be able to maintain **health, safety, and well-being** in the primary private residence or other approved location with both **formal and informal supports**;
- have paid care needs that can be maintained within the **average institutional cost** of the CAP/DA waiver;
- have a **primary physician** who can link and coordinate all medical services; and
- have an **emergency back-up and disaster plan** identifying who will provide care when regular staff or the primary caregiver cannot.

Source: **Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2, Section 3.2.1 — "Specific criteria covered by Medicaid"** (effective Sept. 1, 2025)  
[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

## Plain-language summary
A person is generally eligible for **CAP/DA** if they:

1. **have NC Medicaid**,  
2. meet **nursing-facility level of care**,  
3. need **long-term services and supports** that would otherwise likely be provided in an institution,  
4. can be safely served at home or another approved setting with supports,  
5. have a **service plan**, **primary physician**, and **backup plan**, and  
6. can be served within the waiver’s **cost limits**.

I checked amendment status for this policy, and the current authoritative version I’m citing is **Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2**, effective **September 1, 2025**.

I also see this policy has additional “not covered” subsections nearby, so I’m checking those and pulling the amendment history before I answer.Under **NC Medicaid Clinical Coverage Policy 5B (Orthotics & Prosthetics)**, the policy states that the following are **not covered**:

- **Devices for the beneficiary’s comfort or convenience**, or for the convenience of the beneficiary’s caregiver(s)
- **Backup devices** or **duplicate devices** kept available at different locations
- **Devices and supplies for residents of nursing facilities**
- **Devices or supplies covered by another agency**
- **Equipment or supplies for beneficiaries receiving hospice care**, as defined in the policy’s hospice coordination subsection

Source: **Clinical Coverage Policy 5B, Section 4.2.1 — “Specific Criteria Not Covered by Medicaid”** [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

The policy also says orthotics/prosthetics are **not covered generally** when:

- the beneficiary does **not** meet the eligibility requirements in Section 2.0;
- the beneficiary does **not** meet the coverage criteria in Section 3.0;
- the item or service **duplicates another provider’s** procedure, product, or service; or
- the item or service is **experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial**

Source: **Clinical Coverage Policy 5B, Section 4.1 — “General Criteria Not Covered”** [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

## General criteria that must be met for coverage

For coverage, the policy requires the orthotic/prosthetic item or service to be:

- **individualized, specific, and consistent** with the beneficiary’s symptoms or confirmed diagnosis, and **not in excess of the beneficiary’s needs**
- able to be **safely furnished**
- such that **no equally effective and more conservative or less costly treatment is available statewide**
- furnished in a manner **not primarily intended for convenience** of the beneficiary, caretaker, or provider

Source: **Clinical Coverage Policy 5B, Section 3.1 — “General Criteria Covered”** [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

The policy also gives **specific coverage criteria**. Orthotics/prosthetics must be:

- **ordered by a physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner**
- **medically necessary** to maintain or improve the beneficiary’s medical, physical, or functional level
- **appropriate for use in any noninstitutional setting** where normal life activities take place
- supported by a **documented face-to-face encounter** with the ordering physician, PA, or NP related to the primary reason the beneficiary needs the device, occurring **no more than six months before** initiation
- subject to review of the beneficiary’s need by the ordering physician, PA, or NP **at least annually**

The policy further says:

- **Orthotic devices** are medically necessary when required to **correct or prevent skeletal deformities**, **support or align movable body parts**, or **preserve or improve physical function**
- **Prosthetic devices** are medically necessary as a replacement for all or part of the function of a **permanently inoperative, absent, or malfunctioning body part**, and the beneficiary must require the prosthesis for **mobility, daily care, or rehabilitation purposes**

And orthotic/prosthetic devices must also be:

- a **reasonable and medically necessary** part of the treatment plan
- **consistent with the diagnosis and medical condition**, especially the beneficiary’s functional limitations and symptoms
- of **high quality**, with replacement parts **available and obtainable**

Source: **Clinical Coverage Policy 5B, Section 3.2.1 — “Specific criteria covered by Medicaid”** [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

## Bottom line

**Not covered:** comfort/convenience items, backup/duplicate devices, nursing-facility devices/supplies, items covered by another agency, and hospice-related equipment/supplies under this policy.

**Covered only if:** the device is medically necessary, properly ordered, tied to the beneficiary’s diagnosis and functional needs, not mainly for convenience, no equally effective less costly alternative is available statewide, and the required face-to-face and annual review requirements are met.

I’ve got the current policy version and effective date; next I’m reading the discharge section and checking whether this policy has any change notices that affect what should be cited now.Here are the **entrance, continued service, and discharge criteria** for **NC Medicaid outpatient behavioral health services** under **Clinical Coverage Policy 8C**.

## Short answer

For **outpatient behavioral health services**, NC Medicaid requires that the person meet the policy’s **entrance criteria** to start services, must continue to meet **continued service criteria** to keep receiving them, and should be discharged when one of the policy’s **discharge criteria** is met.

## 1) Entrance criteria

A beneficiary meets the **entrance criteria** if the following are present:

- **A current DSM-5 diagnosis**
- **Behavioral, psychological, or biological dysfunction and functional impairment** consistent with and associated with that diagnosis
- If a **higher level of care is indicated but unavailable**, or the beneficiary is **refusing** that higher level of care, outpatient services may still be provided **until the appropriate level of care is available** or **to support the beneficiary to participate in that higher level of care**
- The beneficiary is **capable of developing skills** to manage symptoms, make behavioral changes, and respond favorably to therapeutic interventions
- There is **no evidence that alternative interventions would be more effective**, based on North Carolina community practice standards

**Citation:** Clinical Coverage Policy 8C, Section 3.2.1.1 — “Entrance Criteria” ([8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)), effective 2025-04-15.

## 2) Continued service criteria

The policy says **continued services** require:

### First, at least one of these:
- The desired outcome or level of functioning **has not been restored, improved, or sustained** over the timeframe in the treatment plan
- The beneficiary **continues to be at risk for relapse** based on current clinical assessment and history
- The beneficiary’s functional gains are **tenuous**

### And, in addition to that, at least one of these:
- The beneficiary has **achieved current treatment plan goals**, and **additional goals are indicated** by documented symptoms; **or**
- The beneficiary is **making satisfactory progress toward meeting goals**, and there is documentation supporting that

**Citation:** Clinical Coverage Policy 8C, Section 3.2.1.2 — “Continued Service Criteria” ([8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)), effective 2025-04-15.

## 3) Discharge criteria

The policy lists discharge when **any one** of these applies:

- The beneficiary’s **level of functioning has improved** with respect to the goals in the treatment plan
- The beneficiary or legally responsible person **no longer wishes to receive** the services
- The beneficiary, based on presentation and **failure to show improvement despite modifications in the treatment plan**, requires a **more appropriate best practice or evidence-based treatment modality** under North Carolina community practice standards

**Citation:** Clinical Coverage Policy 8C, Section 3.2.1.3 — “Discharge Criteria” ([8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)), effective 2025-04-15.

## 4) Broader coverage standard

These service-specific criteria sit on top of the policy’s general Medicaid coverage standard. Policy 8C also says the service must be:

- **Individualized, specific, and consistent** with symptoms or the confirmed diagnosis
- **Not in excess of the beneficiary’s needs**
- Able to be **safely furnished**
- Not replaceable by an **equally effective and more conservative or less costly** treatment available statewide
- Not provided primarily for the **convenience** of the beneficiary, caretaker, or provider

**Citation:** Clinical Coverage Policy 8C, Section 3.0 / 3.1 — “When the Procedure, Product, or Service Is Covered” / “General Criteria Covered” ([8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)), effective 2025-04-15.

per_question.question: How does the EPSDT special provision affect coverage for outpatient therapy services, and what ordering practitioner requirements apply to beneficiaries under 21?

To make sure I answer the EPSDT piece accurately, I’m going to pull the surrounding context and amendment history, because the EPSDT section text in the graph is truncated and I need to confirm how it sits within the current policy.## Short answer

For **beneficiaries under 21**, the **EPSDT special provision** can allow coverage of outpatient therapy services **as an exception to policy limitations**, but it does **not** waive the policy’s core medical-necessity standards or prior-approval rules. The ordering requirement still applies: therapy must be ordered before services start, and the order must come from an authorized ordering practitioner.  
Source: [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

## How EPSDT affects outpatient therapy coverage

Under **Clinical Coverage Policy 10A, Section 2.2.1 — "EPSDT Special Provision: Exception to Policy Limitations for a Medicaid Beneficiary under 21 Years of Age"** ([Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)), Policy 10A recognizes the **EPSDT special provision** for beneficiaries under 21.

Read together with the rest of Policy 10A, that means:

- EPSDT can operate as an **exception to policy limitations** for a Medicaid beneficiary under 21.
- But services still must satisfy the policy’s **general coverage criteria** in **Clinical Coverage Policy 10A, Section 3.1 — "General Criteria Covered"**:
  - the service must be **individualized, specific, and consistent with symptoms or a confirmed diagnosis**;
  - it must **not exceed the beneficiary’s needs**;
  - it must be able to be **safely furnished**;
  - there must be **no equally effective and more conservative or less costly treatment available statewide**; and
  - it cannot be furnished primarily for the **convenience** of the beneficiary, caretaker, or provider.  
  Source: [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

Most importantly, EPSDT matters because Policy 10A’s stated visit caps are written for **beneficiaries 21 and older**. **Clinical Coverage Policy 10A, Section 5.3 — "Visit Limitations Beneficiaries 21 Years of Age and Older"** sets these limits:

- **30 treatment visits per calendar year** combined across **occupational and physical therapy habilitative services**;
- **30 treatment visits per calendar year** combined across **occupational and physical therapy rehabilitative services**;
- **30 treatment visits per calendar year** for **speech therapy habilitative services**; and
- **30 treatment visits per calendar year** for **speech therapy rehabilitative services**.  
Source: [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

### Practical effect for under-21 beneficiaries

So, for a beneficiary **under 21**:

- the adult visit-limit section in **Section 5.3** is not the end of the analysis;
- EPSDT may support coverage **beyond ordinary policy limitations** when medically necessary; but
- EPSDT does **not** eliminate:
  - the need to meet the policy’s substantive coverage standards, or
  - the need for **prior approval** when prior approval is otherwise required.

That last point is explicit in **Clinical Coverage Policy 10A, unnumbered subsection "b. EPSDT and Prior Approval Requirements"**:  
> “If the service, product, or procedure requires prior approval, the fact that the beneficiary is under 21 years of age does NOT eliminate the requirement for prior approval.”  
Source: [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

## Ordering practitioner requirements for beneficiaries under 21

**Clinical Coverage Policy 10A, Section 3.1.2 — "Ordering Practitioners"** lists the authorized ordering practitioners as:

- **Medical Doctor (MD)**
- **Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine (DO)**
- **Doctor of Podiatric Medicine (DPM)**
- **Certified Nurse Midwife (CNM)**
- **Physician Assistant (PA)**
- **Nurse Practitioner (NP)**  
Source: [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

In addition, the treatment-order subsection in Policy 10A states:

- **A verbal or written order must be obtained before services start**;
- verbal orders must include the **date** and **signature of the person receiving the order**;
- verbal orders must be **recorded in the beneficiary’s health record** and **countersigned by the physician within 60 calendar days**;
- verbal orders are valid for **up to six months** from the documented receipt date;
- written orders are valid for **up to six months** from the physician’s signature date;
- **backdating is not allowed**;
- all services must be provided according to a **treatment plan** meeting Policy 10A requirements; and
- **prior approval is required before treatment starts**.  
Source: **Clinical Coverage Policy 10A, unnumbered subsection "Treatment services must adhere to the following requirements:"** ([Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment))

## Bottom line

For **outpatient therapy under Policy 10A**, EPSDT gives beneficiaries **under 21** a route to coverage **beyond ordinary policy limitations**, including limits that are expressly written for adults, but it does **not** remove the need for:

- a covered, medically necessary therapy service under **Section 3.1**;
- an order from an authorized practitioner under **Section 3.1.2**; and
- **prior approval** where the policy requires it.

per_question.question: Does NC Medicaid cover Personal Care Services for beneficiaries who live in an assisted living facility?
per_question.agent_answer:

I’ve checked amendments for 3L-1; I’m doing the same for 3L and pulling one more coverage/eligibility section from 3L-1 so the answer is grounded in both setting and beneficiary criteria.## Yes — NC Medicaid can cover Personal Care Services for someone living in an assisted living facility, but the applicable policy is **Clinical Coverage Policy 3L-1**, not the in-home PCS policy.

**Why:** NC Medicaid has **two different PCS policies**:

- **Clinical Coverage Policy 3L** covers **PCS in in-home settings**. Its coverage section is explicitly titled **“Personal Care Services in In-Home Settings.”** [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3l-state-plan-personal-care-services-pcs/download?attachment)
- **Clinical Coverage Policy 3L-1** covers **PCS provided in congregate settings**, which includes licensed adult care homes. That is the policy that matches an **assisted living / adult care home** setting. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

I am **not using Policy 3L as the primary source** because it governs **in-home settings**, while your question is about an assisted-living-type congregate facility.

## What 3L-1 says

Under **Clinical Coverage Policy 3L-1, Section 3.2.1 — “Specific criteria covered by Medicaid,”** Medicaid covers PCS for a beneficiary who:

- has a medical or mental condition, disability, or cognitive impairment; and
- has unmet needs for at least:
  - **three of the five qualifying ADLs with limited hands-on assistance**, or
  - **two ADLs, one requiring extensive assistance**, or
  - **two ADLs, one requiring full dependence assistance**; and
- **resides in**:
  - **a congregate facility licensed by North Carolina as an Adult Care Home (ACH)** or combination home; or
  - a qualifying supervised living group home.  
  [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

That same section also requires, among other things, that:

- the setting be safe,
- there be no other third-party payer responsible for PCS,
- no informal caregiver is available, willing, and able to provide the authorized services at those times,
- the beneficiary be under the ongoing direct care of a physician for the condition causing the functional limits, and
- the beneficiary be medically stable and **not** require continuous care, monitoring, or supervision by a licensed nurse or other licensed health professional.  
  **Citation:** Clinical Coverage Policy 3L-1, Section 3.2.1 — “Specific criteria covered by Medicaid.” [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

## What services are covered

**Clinical Coverage Policy 3L-1, Section 3.3 — “Personal Care Services”** says Medicaid covers PCS at least once per week, including:

- hands-on assistance with qualifying ADLs,
- related cueing/prompting/guiding when part of that hands-on assistance,
- certain home-management IADLs directly related to the beneficiary’s qualifying ADLs and essential to care at the private residence,
- medication assistance tied to the documented condition or impairment,
- assistance with adaptive/assistive devices,
- assistance with durable medical equipment tied to the qualifying ADLs, and
- special assistance / delegated medical monitoring tasks.  
  **Citation:** Clinical Coverage Policy 3L-1, Section 3.3 — “Personal Care Services.” [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

## Important limit

Even in a licensed congregate facility, PCS is **not covered** for someone whose needs are beyond what that setting can safely meet. Under **Clinical Coverage Policy 3L-1, Section 4.2.1.1 — “Licensed Congregate Facility,”** PCS is not covered if, for example, the person:

- is ventilator dependent,
- requires continuous licensed nursing care,
- has a physician certification that the placement is no longer appropriate, or
- has health, medical, or functional needs that cannot be properly met in the licensed care home.  
  [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

## Bottom line

**Yes.** NC Medicaid **does cover PCS for beneficiaries living in an assisted living facility/adult care home**, **if** the facility is a qualifying licensed congregate setting and the beneficiary meets the functional and medical criteria in **Policy 3L-1**.

Policy 3L shows an effective date of **January 1, 2026**; the database entry for Policy 3L-1 did not provide an effective date.

- The **electronic health record must be transferred** to the receiving county

- Services must be **planned to start on the first date of the transfer into the receiving county**

I’m now reading NC’s introductory CAP/DA section plus a second federal section that usually contains the cost-neutrality and application-content requirements.I found the exact application sections: 42 CFR 441.301 and 441.303. I’ve also confirmed the current authoritative regulation source for Part 441; now I’m reading those sections in full so I can state exactly what the waiver application must show.I now have the main federal application requirements: the state must provide 441.302 assurances plus 441.303 supporting documentation, including evaluations, choice of institutional versus HCBS, and cost neutrality. One remaining gap is the exact statutory citation to the Social Security Act section, so I’m checking whether the NC manual or regulation text expressly ties CAP/DA to section 1915(c).## Short answer

NC’s **CAP/DA waiver** is federally authorized under **section 1915(c) of the Social Security Act**—the Medicaid **home- and community-based services (HCBS) waiver** authority. The federal regulations implementing that authority appear in **42 CFR Part 441, Subpart G**, and the waiver application must include both the required **state assurances** and **supporting documentation** showing that the waiver meets federal standards. See **42 CFR Part 441, Section 441.301 — “Contents of request for a waiver”** and **Section 441.303 — “Supporting documentation required”** ([42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)).

## What the state must demonstrate in its waiver application

Under **42 CFR Part 441, Section 441.301 — “Contents of request for a waiver”** ([42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)), the waiver request must include:

- the **assurances required by 42 CFR 441.302**;
- the **supporting documentation required by 42 CFR 441.303**;
- any requested waivers of certain Medicaid state-plan requirements, when applicable; and
- a statement about whether the state will refuse HCBS to a beneficiary if the expected cost would exceed the cost of an equivalent institutional level of care.

More specifically, the state must show that waiver services will be:

- furnished under a **written person-centered service plan** approved by the Medicaid agency;
- furnished **only to beneficiaries who are not inpatients** of a hospital, nursing facility, or ICF/IID; and
- furnished **only to beneficiaries who, absent waiver services, would require** the Medicaid-covered level of care provided in a hospital, nursing facility, or ICF/IID.

The state also must describe:

- who develops the plan of care;
- the **target group** to be served; and
- each waiver service separately.

## The required federal “showings” / assurances

Under **42 CFR Part 441, Section 441.302 — “State assurances”** ([42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)), CMS will not grant a waiver unless the Medicaid agency gives satisfactory assurances, including:

- **health and welfare** safeguards for beneficiaries;
- **financial accountability** for waiver funds;
- proper **evaluation and reevaluation** of beneficiaries;
- that beneficiaries are informed of **feasible alternatives** and may choose either institutional care or HCBS;
- proper application of **post-eligibility treatment of income** rules where applicable; and
- that the waiver is **cost-neutral** to Medicaid, as required by the federal formula.

From the full text I retrieved, the health-and-welfare assurances specifically include standards for providers, compliance with state licensure/certification requirements, and assurance that services are provided in **home and community-based settings**. **42 CFR Part 441, Section 441.302 — “State assurances”** ([42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)).

## The supporting documentation the application must include

Under **42 CFR Part 441, Section 441.303 — “Supporting documentation required”** ([42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)), the state must furnish CMS with enough information to support those assurances, including:

- a description of **health and welfare safeguards**;
- a description of the **records and information** the state will maintain for financial accountability;
- the state’s plan for **evaluation and reevaluation** of beneficiaries, including:
  - who performs the evaluations,
  - how they are done,
  - the evaluation form used,
  - procedures for maintaining written documentation, and
  - procedures for periodic reevaluations;
- a description of how the state will **inform eligible beneficiaries of feasible alternatives** and allow them to choose between institutional services and HCBS;
- an explanation of how the state will apply the rules on **post-eligibility treatment of income and resources** for certain waiver participants; and
- an explanation, with supporting documentation satisfactory to CMS, of how the state estimated **average per capita expenditures**.

## Cost neutrality: what exactly must be shown

A key part of the application is **cost neutrality**.  
Under **42 CFR Part 441, Section 441.303(f)**, the state must show that:

> “The annual average per capita expenditure estimate of the cost of home and community-based and other Medicaid services under the waiver must not exceed the estimated annual average per capita expenditures of the cost of services in the absence of a waiver.”

The regulation expresses this as:

**D + D′ ≤ G + G′**

That means the projected average Medicaid cost for waiver participants **with the waiver** cannot be greater than the projected average Medicaid cost **without the waiver**. **42 CFR Part 441, Section 441.303 — “Supporting documentation required”** ([42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)).

## NC-specific CAP/DA context

NC’s own CAP policy describes **CAP/DA** as serving adults who are age 18 or older, who meet disability/aging criteria, and who are determined to require an **ICF or SNF level of care**, need CAP services, and live in a private residence. That is consistent with the federal 1915(c) structure requiring a showing that the person would otherwise need institutional level of care. See **DHHS Policy MA-2280 — “Community Alternatives Program (CAP),” subsection “A. CAP for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)”** ([MA-2280 COMMUNITY ALTERNATIVES PROGRAM (CAP)](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2280-2-1-1.pdf)).  
For MA-2280, the most recent amendment returned by the database was **CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 03-20, Community Alternative Program (CAP)**, effective 2020, but its change summary concerns termination-notice procedures rather than the federal authority question ([CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 03-20, Community Alternative Program (CAP)](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/change-notice-03-20-abd-docx.pdf)).

## Bottom line

For NC’s CAP/DA waiver, the federal authority is **Social Security Act § 1915(c)**. In its waiver application, the state must demonstrate to CMS that:

- beneficiaries would otherwise need **institutional level of care**;
- the waiver protects **health and welfare**;
- the state has **financial accountability** systems;
- beneficiaries are evaluated and reevaluated properly;
- beneficiaries are given a real **choice** between institutional care and HCBS;
- services are furnished under a **person-centered plan of care** in **home and community-based settings**; and
- the waiver is **cost-neutral** on an average per-capita basis.

per_question.question: What does federal law define as 'home health services' under Medicaid, and where must they be provided?
per_question.agent_answer:
I found the directly relevant federal regulation: **42 CFR 440.70 — “Home health services.”** Next I’m pulling the full text and checking whether this regulation has any amendments in the corpus before I answer.## Short answer

Under federal Medicaid law, **“home health services”** are the services listed in **42 CFR 440.70(b)** when they are provided:

1. **At the beneficiary’s place of residence**, and  
2. **Pursuant to the required practitioner orders and written plan of care**.  

See **42 CFR 440.70 — “Home health services”** ([42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)).

## What counts as “home health services”

Under **42 CFR 440.70(b)**, home health services include:

- **Nursing services** provided part-time or intermittently
- **Home health aide services**
- **Medical supplies, equipment, and appliances**
- **Physical therapy, occupational therapy, or speech pathology/audiology services** (optional under paragraph (b)(4))

Source: **42 CFR 440.70 — “Home health services”** ([42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)).

## Where they must be provided

Federal law says home health services must be provided **“at [the beneficiary’s] place of residence”**. But the regulation then explains that this is **not limited to a private house** and **not limited to people who are homebound**.

### Excluded settings
A beneficiary’s “place of residence” **does not include**:

- a **hospital**
- a **nursing facility**
- an **intermediate care facility for individuals with intellectual disabilities (ICF/IID)**

There is a narrow exception for certain home health services in an ICF/IID that the facility itself is not required to provide. See **42 CFR 440.70(c)** ([42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)).

### Included settings
The regulation also says nothing in the section should be read to prohibit home health services **“in any setting in which normal life activities take place,”** except the excluded institutional settings above and any setting where Medicaid payment is or could be made for **inpatient services that include room and board**. It also states:

- **Home health services cannot be limited to beneficiaries who are homebound.**

See **42 CFR 440.70(c)(1) — “Home health services”** ([42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)).

## Important procedural elements in the federal definition

Federal law also makes these procedural elements part of the definition:

- For services in **42 CFR 440.70(b)(1), (2), and (4)**, they must be provided on orders written by a **physician, nurse practitioner, clinical nurse specialist, or physician assistant**, working in accordance with state law, and as part of a **written plan of care** reviewed by the ordering practitioner **every 60 days**.
- For **medical supplies, equipment, and appliances** under **42 CFR 440.70(b)(3)**, the rule uses the practitioner/order framework stated in **42 CFR 440.70(a)(3)**, with review as specified in that paragraph and **annual review of need** under **42 CFR 440.70(b)(3)(iii)**.

See **42 CFR 440.70(a) and (b)(3)** ([42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)).

## Plain-language takeaway

Federal Medicaid law defines **home health services** as certain nursing, aide, therapy, and medical-supply/equipment services provided under the required orders and plan of care, **at the beneficiary’s residence or another setting where normal life activities occur**—**not** in a hospital, nursing facility, or most ICF/IID/inpatient room-and-board settings.

For **NC Medicaid hospice**, the policy relies on the federal hospice standard that a person is **terminally ill** if the physician’s prognosis is that the person has a **life expectancy of 6 months or less if the illness runs its normal course**. That exact prognosis standard appears in the federal certification rule for hospice. ### What certification is required?

NC Medicaid requires a **written certification (and later recertifications) of terminal illness**.

#### 1) What the certification must say
Under the federal hospice rule, the certification must state that:

- the individual’s **prognosis is for a life expectancy of 6 months or less** if the terminal illness runs its normal course;
- **clinical information and other documentation** supporting that prognosis must accompany the certification and be in the medical record; and
- the physician must include a **brief narrative explanation of the clinical findings** supporting the prognosis.  
  See **42 CFR Part 418, Section 418.22 — “Certification of terminal illness”** ([42 CFR Part 418](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-418)).

NC Medicaid’s hospice policy adds that the certification or recertification must contain:

- a physician narrative that **briefly synthesizes the clinical information supporting the terminal diagnosis**;
- an attestation that the physician **composed the narrative after reviewing the clinical information** and, where applicable, examining the beneficiary;
- a narrative reflecting the beneficiary’s **individual clinical circumstances**;
- the **election period dates** to which it applies; and
- the certifying or recertifying physician’s **signature and date**.  
  See **Clinical Coverage Policy 3D — “Hospice Services,” Attachment B, Section D — “Certification and Recertification of Terminal Illness”** (effective **2024-03-15**) ([Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment)).

#### 2) Who must sign the **initial** certification
For the **initial 90-day period**, NC Medicaid requires written certification from:

- **the hospice medical director or the physician member of the hospice interdisciplinary group (IDG)**; **and**
- **the individual’s attending physician**, **if** the individual has an attending physician.  

See **Clinical Coverage Policy 3D, Section 5.4.3 — “Sources of certification”** (effective **2024-03-15**) ([Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment)).

#### 3) Who must sign **later recertifications**
For **subsequent periods**, NC Medicaid requires only certification by:

- **the hospice medical director** or
- **the physician member of the hospice interdisciplinary group**.  

See **Clinical Coverage Policy 3D, Section 5.4.3 — “Sources of certification”** ([Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment)).

#### 4) Timing and face-to-face requirement
NC Medicaid’s policy says:

- **Initial certifications** may be prepared **no more than 15 calendar days before** the effective date of election.
- **Recertifications** may be prepared **no more than 15 calendar days before** the start of the subsequent election period.
- For the **third and later election periods**, the narrative must also explain why the **face-to-face encounter** findings support a life expectancy of six months or less.  

See **Clinical Coverage Policy 3D, Attachment B, Section D — “Certification and Recertification of Terminal Illness”** ([Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment)).  
The federal rule similarly requires a face-to-face encounter before the **third benefit period recertification** and each one thereafter. See **42 CFR Part 418, Section 418.22** ([42 CFR Part 418](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-418)).

## Short answer
**“Terminally ill” for NC Medicaid hospice means the patient has a prognosis of 6 months or less to live if the illness runs its normal course.** Hospice eligibility requires a **written physician certification of terminal illness** supported by clinical documentation and a physician narrative. For the **initial period**, certification must come from the **hospice medical director or hospice IDG physician**, plus the **attending physician if there is one**; for **later periods**, only the **hospice medical director or hospice IDG physician** is required.

The service must meet NC Medicaid’s general medical-necessity standards. The policy says the service must be:

- **individualized, specific, and consistent with symptoms or a confirmed diagnosis** and **not in excess of the beneficiary’s needs**;
- able to be **safely furnished**, with **no equally effective and more conservative or less costly treatment available statewide**; and
- furnished in a manner **not primarily intended for the convenience** of the beneficiary, caretaker, or provider.

For CAR-T itself, Medicaid covers it only when all of these are met:

- the **CAR T-Cell Therapy has received U.S. FDA approval**;
- it is administered according to **FDA-approved guidelines** for:
  - **indications and usage**;
  - **dosage and administration**;
  - **dosage forms and strengths**; and
  - **warnings and precautions**;
- it is administered at a **certified or authorized treatment center**; and
- if the therapy is subject to a **REMS** program, the treatment center must be **enrolled in the REMS**, and providers must be **trained to manage cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and neurological toxicities**.

The policy also requires:

- hospitals and associated clinics that dispense CAR-T therapies to be **specially certified** and to have **on-site, immediate access to tocilizumab**; and
- those who prescribe, dispense, or administer CAR-T therapies to be **aware of how to manage the risks of CRS and neurological toxicities**.

- **enrolled in the NC Medicaid Program**; and
- not subject to an **eligibility-category restriction** that would make them ineligible for this service.

- the beneficiary is receiving **repeat treatment** after previously receiving another CAR-T cell therapy;

## Bottom line
In plain language, NC Medicaid covers CAR-T therapy only if:

1. the **specific CAR-T product is FDA-approved**;
2. it is used **exactly within FDA-approved parameters**;
3. it is given at a **properly certified/authorized center**, including **REMS enrollment** when required;
4. the center and clinicians can manage **CRS and neurologic toxicity**, including **immediate access to tocilizumab**;

I’m pulling the training and supervisor-experience sections because decertification expressly ties back to those staffing criteria.## HIV case management provider certification and decertification under NC Medicaid

The governing source is **Clinical Coverage Policy 12B, Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Case Management**, effective **January 15, 2020**: [Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Case Management](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment).

### Short answer

To be certified as an NC Medicaid **HIV Case Management** provider, an agency must meet the provider certification standards in **Policy 12B, Section 6.2.1**, including:

- **3 years’ documented success** providing or managing HIV case management programs;
- use of **qualified HIV case managers** and **qualified supervisors**;
- **enrollment of each physical site** with NC Medicaid;
- compliance with **state and federal Medicaid participation laws**;
- compliance with **initial and ongoing certification processes**;
- a **quality improvement plan** with case-record monitoring;
- agreement to allow **record, operational, and financial review** by NC Medicaid or its contractor;
- timely notice of **ownership/name/address/phone/business-dissolution changes**; and
- **national accreditation within 1 year of Medicaid enrollment** from one of the listed accrediting bodies.

A provider may be **decertified** for any of the grounds listed in **Policy 12B, Section 6.2.5**, including failure to provide core services, fraudulent billing, felony conviction of owners, falsification of records, confidentiality violations, unqualified or untrained staff, inadequate supervision, insufficient documentation, failure to maintain a quality improvement program, failure to report agency changes, failure to comply with law/policy, failure to enroll beneficiaries within 4 months of certification, or failure to maintain the certification requirements.

---

## 1. Certification requirements

### A. Core provider certification standards

**Clinical Coverage Policy 12B, Section 6.2.1 — “Certification Requirements”** states that the provider must:

- have a **documented successful record of three (3) years** of providing or managing HIV Case Management programs;
- ensure services are provided by **qualified case managers** under **Sections 6.1.1, 6.1.2, and 6.1.3**;
- ensure supervision by **qualified supervisors** under **Sections 6.1.4 and 6.1.5**;
- **enroll each physical site** with NC Medicaid as an HIV Case Management provider;
- meet **applicable state and federal laws** governing Medicaid providers;
- **maintain certification** as a qualified HIV Case Management provider;
- demonstrate compliance with **initial and ongoing certification**;
- demonstrate compliance with **monitoring and evaluation of case management records through a quality improvement plan**;
- allow NC Medicaid or its designated contractor to **review beneficiary records and inspect agency operation and financial records**;
- notify NC Medicaid or its contractor of proposed changes such as **owner, name, address, telephone number, or business dissolution** within **30 calendar days of the proposed change** and no later than **5 business days after the actual change**; and
- **within one year of Medicaid enrollment**, achieve national accreditation from one of these agencies:
  - ACHC
  - CARF
  - CHAP
  - COA
  - PHAB
  - The Joint Commission
  - URAC

**Citation:** **Clinical Coverage Policy 12B, Section 6.2.1 — “Certification Requirements”**: [Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Case Management](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

---

### B. Staffing qualifications required for certification

Because Section 6.2.1 requires **qualified case managers and supervisors**, those staffing rules are part of certification.

#### Qualified HIV case managers
Under **Clinical Coverage Policy 12B, Section 6.1.1 — “HIV Case Manager”**, a case manager must meet one of the listed educational/professional pathways, including:

- a **master’s degree** in a human services field;
- a **bachelor’s degree in social work**;
- a **bachelor’s degree in a human services field or related curriculum** with at least **15 semester hours** related to social work, counseling, or public health, **plus 6 months of social work or counseling experience**;
- a **bachelor’s degree** plus **1 year of experience** in counseling or a related human services field; or
- if applicable, NC licensure as a **registered nurse, nurse practitioner, physician, physician assistant, or certified substance abuse counselor**, plus **2 years of experience working in human services**.

**Citation:** **Clinical Coverage Policy 12B, Section 6.1.1 — “HIV Case Manager”**: [Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Case Management](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

#### Qualified supervisors
Under **Clinical Coverage Policy 12B, Section 6.1.4 — “HIV Case Management Supervisor”**, the supervisor must meet one of several degree/licensure-and-experience combinations, such as:

- a **master’s degree in a human services field** and **1 year of human services experience**;
- a **bachelor’s degree in social work** and **2 years of human services experience**;
- a **bachelor’s degree in a human services field or related curriculum** with at least **15 semester hours** in social work or counseling and **2 years of experience in human services or public health**;
- a **bachelor’s degree** and either **3 years of human services experience**, or **2 years of human services experience plus 1 year of supervisory experience**; or
- applicable NC licensure as **RN, NP, physician, PA, or certified substance abuse counselor**, with either **3 years of human services experience** or **2 years plus 1 year of supervisory experience**.

Section **6.1.5** adds that the supervisor must be able to direct and evaluate case management services, know case management principles and practices, conduct analytical evaluations, and apply professional knowledge of federal and state assistance programs for the HIV-positive population.

**Citations:**  
- **Clinical Coverage Policy 12B, Section 6.1.4 — “HIV Case Management Supervisor”**: [Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Case Management](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)  
- **Clinical Coverage Policy 12B, Section 6.1.5 — “Case Management Supervisor’s Experience”**: [Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Case Management](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

---

### C. Training requirements tied to certification

The policy also ties provider certification to staff training.

Under **Clinical Coverage Policy 12B, Section 6.1.7.1 — “Training for Case Managers and Supervisors”**, training must cover:

- basic HIV information and prevention techniques;
- the scope of work for case managers;
- the core components of HIV Case Management;
- basic ethical issues relating to case management;
- responsibilities and functions of the HIV Case Management system of care; and
- documentation requirements under **Sections 7.5 and 7.6**.

Under **Section 6.1.7.2 — “Annual Training”**, annual training must include:

- confidentiality;
- cultural competency;
- current trends in HIV disease management;
- ethics;
- refresher core components of case management; and
- treatment of individuals who are HIV positive.

The policy states that **six hours of the twelve-hour annual requirement** must be **clinically oriented training (clinical updates)**.

**Citations:**  
- **Clinical Coverage Policy 12B, Section 6.1.7.1 — “Training for Case Managers and Supervisors”**: [Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Case Management](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)  
- **Clinical Coverage Policy 12B, Section 6.1.7.2 — “Annual Training”**: [Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Case Management](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

### D. Application / initial certification materials

The policy’s extracted text for **Section 6.2.3 — “Initial Certification”** is blank in the database, so I cannot quote that section directly. But the nearby certification checklist text in Policy 12B shows the provider must submit at least these materials:

#### Administrative requirements
The policy’s administrative checklist requires:

- list of **counties to be served**;
- **hours of operation**;
- **emergency after-hours response plan**;
- list of **potential community resources** for the service area;
- **Articles of Incorporation** unless the agency is a local government unit;
- a **physical business site** verified by site visit, not in a private residence or vehicle;
- **organizational chart**;
- list of persons with **5% or more ownership**;
- access to **NCCCN, Inc.’s web-based applications**;
- a **business plan** with development costs, projected monthly revenue/expenses for 12 months after approval, and actual revenue/expenses for the prior 12 months, including management structure/resumes, development timetable, and financial resources;
- computer capability to meet **IT, HIPAA, electronic records, data analysis, electronic billing, EFT, and provider communication** requirements;
- completion of a **precertification onsite visit**;
- compliance with **state and federal licensure/certification requirements**; and
- written organizational policies on:
  - confidentiality (including informed consent),
  - grievance,
  - beneficiary rights,
  - non-discrimination,
  - code of ethics,
  - conflict of interest,
  - electronic records,
  - medical records/retention/security,
  - freedom of choice,
  - transfer/discharge,
  - abuse/neglect/exploitation.

**Citation:** **Clinical Coverage Policy 12B, unnumbered section “a. Administrative Requirements”**: [Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Case Management](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

#### Case management program requirements
The policy also requires:

- a description of the **core components** in **Section 5.6** and the titles/positions of the people performing them;
- documentation of sufficient **FTEs or functions** to meet requirements; and
- a **quality improvement plan** addressing:
  - measuring beneficiary health outcomes,
  - monitoring/evaluating case management records,
  - tracking/reporting complaints and resolutions,
  - statistical studies including cost and utilization,
  - accuracy of claims and service records, and
  - ensuring provider/staff meet policy qualifications.

**Citation:** **Clinical Coverage Policy 12B, unnumbered section “b. Case Management Requirements”**: [Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Case Management](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

---

### E. Recertification requirements

Under **Clinical Coverage Policy 12B, Section 6.2.4 — “Recertification”**, the provider must:

- submit a **complete and signed Recertification Application** within **60 calendar days of receipt**;
- submit copies of all items in **Section 6.2.3** that have changed since initial certification;
- submit copies of all **HIV case manager and supervisor credentials**;
- submit **annual summary/summaries of quality improvement activities**, including outcome metrics; and
- submit to a **recertification on-site visit**, including review of beneficiary records or other clinical/business documentation as needed.

**Citation:** **Clinical Coverage Policy 12B, Section 6.2.4 — “Recertification”**: [Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Case Management](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

---

## 2. Grounds for decertification

**Clinical Coverage Policy 12B, Section 6.2.5 — “Decertification”** lists the following grounds. A provider can be decertified for:

1. **Failure to provide core service components**.  
2. **Fraudulent billing practices**.  
3. **Owner(s) being convicted of a felony charge**.  
4. **Failure to develop, submit, and implement a written plan of correction** to resolve unmet program requirements cited by NC Medicaid or its contractor, or failure to make recommended corrections, within **30 calendar days**.  
5. **Falsification of records**.  
6. **Violation of a beneficiary’s confidentiality**.  
7. **Employment of staff who do not meet the criteria** in **Section 6.1**.  
8. **Failure of staff to complete mandatory basic training within 90 days of employment**.  
9. **Failure of staff to obtain required continuing educational units (CEU)** as specified in **Section 6.1**.  
10. **Failure to provide case management staff with supervision** sufficient to meet beneficiaries’ needs.  
11. **Failure to submit required documentation** within the time frame designated by the policy, NC Medicaid, or its contractor.  
12. **Failure to provide documentation sufficient to support billing**, as required by **Section 7.5**.  
13. **Failure to implement and enforce a quality improvement program**.  
14. **Failure to notify NC Medicaid or its contractor** of changes in agency name, director/ownership, mailing address, or telephone number within the required timeframes, resulting in inability to contact the provider.  
15. **Failure to comply with applicable federal and state laws, regulations, the state reimbursement plan, and Medicaid policies**.  
16. **Failure to enroll any beneficiaries within four months of certification**.  
17. **Failure to achieve or maintain the certification requirements** in **Section 6.2**.

**Citation:** **Clinical Coverage Policy 12B, Section 6.2.5 — “Decertification”**: [Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Case Management](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

---

## Practical takeaway

In plain language, NC Medicaid expects an HIV case management provider to be a **formally organized, accredited, site-enrolled agency** with:

- documented HIV case-management program experience,
- qualified and trained staff,
- qualified supervision,
- a working quality-improvement system,
- adequate records and billing support,
- onsite review readiness, and
- timely reporting of organizational changes.

A provider is at risk of decertification if it **fails on service delivery, staff qualifications/training, documentation, supervision, compliance, quality assurance, or basic program integrity requirements**.
